overview: Ventia is a leading essential infrastructure services provider in Australia and New Zealand, formed in 2015 as a carve-out from Leighton Holdings and dual-listed on the ASX (primary) and NZX (secondary) since November 2021. The company operates across four sectors — Defence and Social Infrastructure, Infrastructure Services, Telecommunications, and Transport — delivering long-term operations, maintenance and management of critical public and private assets for government agencies and blue-chip customers via a workforce of more than 35,000 employees and subcontractors across 400+ sites. FY2025 revenue was A$6,141.1m with underlying NPATA of A$257.6m and a record A$22.1bn of work in hand.

business_model.summary: Ventia earns revenue almost entirely from long-term, contracted outsourced maintenance, operations and asset-management services rather than one-off construction — a defensive, annuity-like model with high renewal rates (82% FY25, 98.5% in H1 FY2026) and a large ~A$21-22bn order book providing multi-year revenue visibility (87% of FY26 revenue already secured at H1 results). Growth comes from three levers management explicitly tracks: renewing/growing existing contracts, winning new work (a 'significant win' is defined as >A$100m), and cross-selling capabilities across sectors. Margins are thin but expanding (Group underlying EBITDA margin 8.7% FY25, up from 8.2% FY24; 9.4% in H1 FY2026) reflecting a portfolio shift toward higher-margin work (Energy, Water, Resources) versus lower-margin, more transactional Defence Base Services and construction-adjacent work.
business_model.customer_type: B2G/B2B — government agencies (Australian Department of Defence, state road/water/transport authorities, councils, nbn Co) and large corporates (Telstra, Optus, TransGrid, BHP, AusNet, APA Group, BlueScope); no meaningful direct consumer exposure
business_model.geographic_mix: Australia and New Zealand only; Australia is the large majority given Defence, NBN and major state infrastructure contracts, with New Zealand contributing via Transpower, Tuatahi First Fibre, Far North District Council and other regional/local government contracts

competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest essential infrastructure services (outsourced maintenance) providers in Australia and New Zealand, holding a market share broadly comparable to Downer EDI and CIMIC/UGL within an addressable market Oxford Economics values at A$86.8bn in FY25, forecast to exceed A$100bn by FY28-29 (4.7% CAGR). Ventia is the largest telecommunications infrastructure services provider in Australia/NZ and the leader in incident response for transport networks.

moat_factors.factor: Long-duration contract book and switching costs
moat_factors.description: A$21-22bn work in hand, multi-year (often 5-10+ year) contracts with government and blue-chip customers create high switching costs and revenue visibility; customer renewal rate of 82-98.5% demonstrates entrenchment.

35,000-strong combined workforce across 400+ sites in Australia and New Zealand allows rapid mobilisation for large, complex, geographically dispersed contracts (e.g. nbn's national Field Module contract) that smaller competitors cannot service.

36+ year relationship with the Australian Department of Defence and long histories with major utilities/telcos create trust and repeat-work advantages in panel and tender processes, though outsourcing contracts are periodically re-tendered.
Exposure spread across Defence, Infrastructure Services (energy/water/resources), Telecommunications and Transport reduces reliance on any single end market's investment cycle.
Baa2 (Moody's) / BBB (S&P) ratings support bidding for large government contracts requiring balance-sheet strength and bonding capacity (A$835m of bank guarantee/insurance bond facilities).

weaknesses: Low overall margins (~9% EBITDA margin) typical of a labour-intensive outsourced-services model with limited pricing power on fixed-price/unit-rate contracts
Revenue concentration risk in Defence and Social Infrastructure (39% of FY25 revenue), which saw a 7.0% FY25 and 20% H1 FY2026 revenue decline as contracts transitioned/were re-scoped
Negative net tangible assets per share (-$0.80 at H1 FY2026) reflecting goodwill-heavy balance sheet from the Broadspectrum and other acquisitions
Thin margins leave earnings exposed to cost overruns, wage inflation and contract mispricing, especially given complex industrial-instrument-driven payroll
Ongoing ACCC cartel litigation creates reputational and financial-penalty overhang, and could affect future Defence tender eligibility

growth_drivers: Structural growth in the addressable market: Oxford Economics forecasts Australia/NZ outsourced maintenance services market growing from A$86.8bn (FY25) to A$104.4bn by FY29 (4.7% CAGR), with outsourcing penetration expected to hold near 59% through FY29

Defence spending uplift: Australian Government reaffirmed commitment to lift Defence spending above 2.3% of GDP by 2033-34, and Ventia has just been awarded ~A$2.7bn (Base Services Transformation, commencing Feb 2026) and ~A$935m (Defence Clothing Services, commencing May 2026) Defence contracts that will ramp through FY26-27

Digital infrastructure and telecommunications: nbn Field Module contract (~A$2.1bn, 5yr+2x1yr options), nbn Fibre to the Node upgrade (~A$1.1bn / ~A$800m), and new Optus national contracts (~A$110m) position Ventia to benefit from continued fibre upgrades and growth in data-centre-driven connectivity demand

Energy transition and water security: growth in Energy and Water sub-sectors (grid connection works for wind/solar farms, transmission network maintenance for TransGrid/Transpower/Powerlink, water utility contracts including the new 9-year, A$405m Yarra Valley Water renewal) as networks are built out and aged infrastructure requires more maintenance

Cross-selling and 'whole-of-Ventia' bidding: management strategy explicitly targets bringing multiple service capabilities to existing customers to increase wallet share without new customer acquisition costs

Capital-light growth plus capital returns: strong operating cash conversion (>90%) funds both reinvestment and an expanding on-market share buyback (increased to A$300m cumulative through 2025-2026) alongside a progressive, highly franked dividend (60-80% of NPATA payout policy)

AI and digital productivity tools (VenSpark ideation platform, VenSights analytics, agentic AI for supplier screening/onboarding, PicSure AI photo-QA) targeted at margin expansion through productivity rather than revenue growth

business.risk: Defence and Social Infrastructure revenue decline
business.description: D&SI revenue fell 7.0% in FY25 and 20.0% in H1 FY2026 as the legacy Defence Base Services contract transitioned to the new Base Services Contract and Housing/Community contract scope was reduced; while new Defence contracts (BST, Clothing Services) are large, ramp timing risk exists through FY26-27.

Company explicitly flags that customers may shift from outsourcing to insourcing, competition may intensify, panel-tender wins may not convert to actual work, and contract commencement can be delayed — a structural risk given the business model depends on repeated re-tendering of multi-year contracts.

35,000-strong workforce, including in remote/high-risk environments; a fatality occurred at Port Kembla steelworks in November 2025, underscoring ongoing operational safety exposure with reputational and regulatory consequences.

business.risk: Cyber security and third-party technology dependency
business.description: Complex ICT platform underpins service delivery; a cyber incident could cause operational disruption, data loss and loss of customer trust, potentially impacting the ability to win future government work.

financial.description: Net debt rose to A$748.3m at H1 FY2026 (+A$44.4m) on higher capex and buyback spending; the company issued its first A$300m AMTN notes (7-year, 6.283% coupon) in June 2026, adding fixed-rate debt at a materially higher cost than bank facilities, with leverage covenant of ≤3.25x and interest cover ≥4.0x.

NTA per share was -$0.80 at H1 FY2026 (from -$0.73 at FY25 and -$0.59 at FY24), driven by acquisition goodwill; while common for services roll-ups, it limits balance-sheet asset backing in a downside scenario.

Equity fell from A$630.9m to A$561.1m in FY25 despite A$272.2m of statutory profit, driven by A$137.6m of buybacks (further A$48.2m in H1 FY2026, cumulative A$185.8m since 2025) plus dividends — aggressive capital return reduces balance-sheet buffer if the cycle turns.
Net working capital increases in H1 each year due to seasonally higher volumes in May-June, creating intra-year cash flow variability.

regulatory.description: The ACCC has civil cartel proceedings against Ventia Australia Pty Ltd, Spotless Facility Services (Downer EDI subsidiary) and four senior executives (including two current/former Ventia executives) alleging price-fixing on Defence estate maintenance contracts across 200+ ADF bases between 2019-2022. Trial is set down for 30 days commencing 30 May 2027. Potential financial penalties, reputational damage and risk to future Defence tender eligibility.

Operates under federal, state and local laws across Australia and New Zealand; regulatory or policy changes (e.g. procurement rules, industrial relations law) can affect financial performance and compliance costs.
Large frontline workforce covered by varied industrial instruments, awards and enterprise agreements creates risk of underpayment/overpayment, industrial action, and payroll remediation costs.
Reports under Australia's AASB S2 climate standard; currently holds an NZ FMA exemption from dual climate-reporting requirements, but this could be revisited.

macro.risk: Government fiscal policy and infrastructure spending cycles
macro.description: Heavy reliance on government and quasi-government customers (Defence, NBN, water utilities, road authorities) makes revenue sensitive to public infrastructure budget cycles, though outsourcing trend and essential-services nature of work provide some counter-cyclical resilience.
Rising net debt and a newly issued fixed-rate note (6.283% coupon) increase finance cost exposure; H1 FY2026 finance costs rose 14.2% YoY partly from higher rates and higher debt.
Tight-to-easing but still competitive Australia/NZ labour markets affect wage costs and ability to staff large mobilisations (e.g. new Defence and nbn contracts) on time and on budget.

macro.risk: Extreme weather and climate physical risk
macro.description: Increasing frequency/severity of extreme weather (e.g. Cyclone Alfred) exposes transport and utility assets Ventia maintains to disruption, though this can also generate incremental resilience-upgrade work.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The Australian/NZ outsourced infrastructure maintenance market is forecast to grow at a 4.7% CAGR from A$86.8bn (FY25) to A$104.4bn (FY29), per Oxford Economics Australia, driven by population growth, an ageing asset base, the energy transition, digital infrastructure build-out (fibre, data centres) and a structural increase in Defence spending toward >2.3% of GDP by 2033-34. Investment mix is shifting away from transport (which saw elevated recent spend) toward social infrastructure, defence, energy and utilities.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderately defensive — the business is weighted toward essential maintenance and operations of long-lived public/critical infrastructure assets rather than discretionary new-build construction, and O&M demand is more resilient than capex cycles; however, order intake and contract renewal timing can still be lumpy and government-budget dependent.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — net debt of ~A$748m plus lease liabilities and a newly issued A$300m fixed-rate note mean higher rates increase finance costs; capital-intensive buyback and dividend program is partly debt-funded.
key_input_costs: Plant and equipment (rig and well services capex)

recent_developments.event: Mark Ralston (12-year Ventia veteran, most recently head of Defence & Social Infrastructure) formally commenced as Managing Director and Group CEO, succeeding Dean Banks, who is planning to leave the company in Q4 2026 to return to the UK. Succession followed an extensive internal and external process.

H1 FY2026 results: revenue fell 4.7% YoY to A$2,893.6m (mainly reflecting the Defence Base Services contract transition), but underlying EBITDA rose 8.2% to A$273.3m and underlying NPATA rose 7.4% to A$128.2m, with Group underlying EBITDA margin improving to a record 9.4% (from 8.3%). Work in hand grew to A$21.1bn (+2.5%) and customer renewal rate reached 98.5%. Interim dividend declared at 11.76 cps, 100% franked, a 75% NPATA payout. Shares rose ~4.7% to A$5.83 on the results, near the top of the 52-week range.
First issuance under Ventia's Australian Medium Term Notes (AMTN) Programme: A$300m of 7-year fixed-rate notes at a 6.283% coupon, maturing 2033, diversifying funding away from bank facilities.

On-market share buyback increased to a cumulative A$300m across 2025-2026 (from an initial A$150m FY25 buyback); as of early September 2026, ~A$185.8m had been used to repurchase 37.7 million shares at an average A$4.93, with daily repurchases continuing (e.g. 163,182 shares bought on 1 September 2026 at A$5.40-5.50).

New multi-year contract wins/extensions disclosed through H1 FY2026: nine-year, A$405m Yarra Valley Water maintenance renewal; five-year, A$133m extension for the Australian Marine Complex-Common User Facility (WA); two-year Transpower New Zealand extension; ~A$110m of new national Optus contracts; four-year Victorian Road Maintenance Contracts (Metro-East and Grampians, mobilised 1 July 2026); and a five-year, NZ$125m Far North District Council renewal.

FY2025 full-year results: revenue of A$6,141.1m (+0.6%), statutory NPAT of A$272.2m (+23.6%), underlying NPATA of A$257.6m (+13.0%), record work in hand of A$22.1bn (+14.4%) including A$8.2bn won during the year. Total FY25 dividend of 23.25 cps (75% NPATA payout, 90% franked). Management issued FY26 guidance for underlying NPATA growth of 7-10% (excluding the one-off A$24.9m TSRC novation gain), and announced a further A$100m to be deployed under the buyback in 2026 (bringing the cumulative program to A$250m at the time, later increased to A$300m).

ACCC civil cartel proceedings against Ventia Australia Pty Ltd, Downer subsidiary Spotless Facility Services, and senior executives (including current/former Ventia staff) alleging price-fixing on Australian Defence Force estate-maintenance contracts (2019-2022) remain before the Federal Court, with a 30-day trial listed to commence 30 May 2027.

Original private equity sponsors continued to exit: as of September 2025, Apollo Global Management's stake had fallen to ~4.32% and CIMIC Group's to ~7.35%, down from 32.8% each at IPO (November 2021) and 15% each in May 2023 — removing a long-running overhang of sponsor selldowns on the stock.

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2026 results (24 August 2026), reaffirming FY2025 annual report guidance (19 February 2026)

items.notes: Guidance excludes the one-off positive A$24.9m impact of the FY2025 Toowoomba Second Range Crossing (TSRC) novation gain, i.e. growth is measured off the A$257.6m FY25 underlying NPATA base. Reaffirmed at H1 FY2026 results alongside underlying NPATA of A$128.2m (+7.4% YoY) for the half.
Reflects the long-term, contracted nature of the order book; supports confidence in the NPATA growth guidance despite the Defence Base Services revenue transition headwind.
H1 FY2026 conversion was 93.8% (statutory) / 93.8% underlying, ahead of the >90% target and up from 85.7%/93.2% in H1 FY2025.
H1 FY2026 interim dividend of 11.76 cps (100% franked) represented a 75% payout ratio, consistent with FY2025's 75% payout (23.25 cps total, 90% franked).

items.vs_prior: raised — increased from A$150m (Aug 2025) to a cumulative A$250m (Feb 2026 annual report) to A$300m (by mid-2026)
items.notes: A$185.8m deployed by early September 2026 (37.7m shares at avg A$4.93); buyback continuing into H2 2026 at higher average prices (~A$5.40-5.65) as the stock has re-rated.

guidance.management_commentary: H1 FY2026 outlook statement: 'The outlook for the second half of 2026 remains positive, supported by the Group's diversified and resilient portfolio, favourable market conditions and continued execution of our strategy to Redefine Service Excellence.' Management highlighted the 98.5% customer renewal rate, a A$21.1bn work-in-hand base, and structural tailwinds in defence, digital infrastructure, energy transition and water security as underpinning 'confidence in the Group's ability to deliver sustainable earnings growth while continuing to create shareholder value through a growing dividend profile.' FY2025 annual report Chairman/CEO letter emphasised the $86.8bn addressable market (forecast to exceed $100bn by FY28) and intent to pursue 'close to core' adjacent-market opportunities while balancing risk.

bull_case: Highly defensive, contracted revenue base: ~A$21bn work in hand, 82-98.5% customer renewal rates and 87% of FY26 revenue already secured give strong multi-year earnings visibility uncommon among industrial services peers

Margin expansion story intact: Group underlying EBITDA margin has risen from 8.2% (FY24) to 8.7% (FY25) to a record 9.4% (H1 FY2026) as the portfolio mix shifts toward higher-margin Energy, Water and Infrastructure Services work, with further upside from AI/digital productivity initiatives (VenSpark, VenSights, agentic AI)

Structural demand tailwinds across all four sectors: rising Australian Defence spending (>2.3% of GDP by 2033-34) has already delivered ~A$2.7bn and ~A$935m of new Defence contracts; energy transition, water security investment and digital infrastructure (fibre, data centres) all support the A$86.8bn to >A$100bn addressable market growth through FY28-29

Removal of sponsor overhang plus aggressive capital returns: Apollo and CIMIC have sold down from 32.8% each at IPO to ~4.3%/7.4% respectively, while the company simultaneously runs an expanding buyback (now A$300m cumulative) and a highly franked dividend (75% NPATA payout), directly supporting the share price and EPS growth

Smooth, internally-promoted leadership transition: new CEO Mark Ralston is a 12-year Ventia veteran who most recently led the largest sector (Defence & Social Infrastructure), reducing execution/strategy-continuity risk versus an external hire
bear_case: Defence and Social Infrastructure — Ventia's largest sector at 39% of FY25 revenue — is in the midst of a disruptive contract transition, with revenue down 7.0% in FY25 and a steep 20.0% in H1 FY2026; the large new BST and Clothing Services contracts carry ramp-up and margin execution risk before they offset the legacy contract runoff

ACCC cartel litigation is a live, material overhang: civil proceedings allege Ventia and a Downer subsidiary price-fixed Defence estate-maintenance contracts across 200+ bases (2019-2022), with a 30-day Federal Court trial not scheduled until May 2027 — creating a prolonged period of uncertainty over penalties and potential reputational damage to Ventia's largest customer relationship

Structurally thin margins (~9% EBITDA) leave limited room for error on a labour-intensive, fixed-price/unit-rate contract book exposed to wage inflation, complex industrial-instrument payroll risk, and potential contract mispricing or delivery failures

Rising leverage and finance costs alongside an aggressive buyback: net debt increased to A$748.3m (H1 FY2026) and the company issued its first fixed-rate notes at a 6.283% coupon; equity fell from A$630.9m to A$561.1m in FY25 despite A$272.2m of profit as buybacks and dividends outpaced retained earnings, reducing the balance-sheet buffer

Heavy dependence on government/quasi-government counterparties (Defence, NBN, state transport and water authorities) exposes revenue to public-sector budget cycles, insourcing risk, and the possibility that large panel/tender wins fail to convert into actual awarded work as flagged explicitly in the company's own risk disclosures
